summary.text: A review pool for all of Topic 2 (lessons 2-1 through 2-7): mental strategies, estimation, the addition and subtraction algorithms, checks, and across-zero subtraction — plus a spiral of Topic 1 place value, comparing and rounding, because the tests mix old and new.

why.text: The class's tests spiral earlier topics on purpose, so a review that only rehearses the newest material practises for a test that will not exist. Six of these questions reach back to Topic 1 — deciding which topic a question even belongs to is part of the skill.

objectives.text: Add and subtract multi-digit numbers, mentally and with the algorithm
Estimate first and use the estimate to judge exact answers
Check subtraction with the inverse addition, forwards and backwards
Keep Topic 1 place value, comparing and rounding warm

parentNote.text: A review pool, not a lesson: 24 fresh questions served 12 per sitting — 18 across all seven Topic 2 lessons plus 6 that spiral Topic 1, matching the syllabus note that most tests spiral earlier material. Approve it when the class heads into review days before the Topic 2 test. Two sittings cover the pool; misses ride the Growth Zone ladder as usual. Error-diagnosis questions (the flip, the fix-up direction) mirror the test's explain-your-thinking items.

nextUp.text: Twelve questions per sitting, mixing all of Topic 2 with a taste of Topic 1 — like the real test.

cards.def:
**Break apart, compensation, counting up — reshape first, compute second.**
• Close numbers: count up. One near-round number: compensate. Otherwise: break apart.
• Three seconds of choosing saves thirty of grinding.

**Compensation's fix-up UNDOES the trade — it never repeats it.**
• Added too much? Subtract it back. Subtracted too much? Add it back.
• Say the direction out loud before touching the numbers.
cards.hint: Ask: did my trade make the answer too big or too small?

cards.def:
**Round first for an estimate, work exactly, then compare the two.**
• Close together: trust the exact answer. Far apart: find the mistake.
• This three-beat rhythm is the whole discipline of Topic 2.

**A carry bundles 10 into 1 of the next place; a borrow breaks 1 into 10 of this one.**
• Same trade, opposite directions — and the number's value never changes.
• If you can narrate the trade, you own the algorithm.

**Difference + what you subtracted = what you started with.**
• Every subtraction is a checkable claim, and the check is one easy addition.
• A failed check is a verdict, not a suggestion.

**Middle zeros become 9s when a borrow ripples through — or slide both numbers down 1 and skip it all.**
• 6,000 − 4,678 = 5,999 − 4,677: same gap, zero borrows.
• A difference is a gap, and gaps ignore where they sit.

**Rounding, comparing and place value never left — every estimate in Topic 2 is Topic 1 working.**
• The test will mix old and new on purpose. So does this review.
• If a rounding feels rusty, revisit the Topic 1 shelf first.

questions.hint: Trade 3,999 for a friendlier number.

ex.main: **6,467.** Compensation — borrow a 1, use it, give it back.
ex.tip: Near-round numbers are invitations. 3,999 is begging to be 4,000 for a moment.

questions.hint: Round each number on its own digit.

ex.main: **12,000.** The exact sum, 12,131, lands right beside it.
ex.tip: One rounded down, one rounded up — never round as a package deal.

questions.hint: Two carries coming.

ex.main: **823.** Both carries were real tens and hundreds in transit.
ex.tip: Estimate check: 400 + 400 = 800. Close, so 823 is trustworthy.

questions.hint: Five columns, same trades.
steps: Hundreds: 4 + 6 = 10. Write 0, carry 1. Thousands: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1.

ex.main: **64,091.** The algorithm scaled up without changing a single rule.
ex.tip: Estimate: 35,000 + 29,000 = 64,000. The exact answer parks right next to it.

questions.hint: Both the ones and tens will borrow.

ex.main: **376.** Check: 376 + 258 = 634 — the pieces rebuild the start.
ex.tip: The wrong answer 424 is the flip error. If no column ever seems to need a borrow, be suspicious.

questions.hint: Scout the columns first: which will borrow?
steps: Ones: 5 − 8 — trade: 15 − 8 = 7. Tens: 0 − 3 after lending — the 0 borrows: 9 − 3 = 6.
Hundreds: 4 − 1 after lending = 2... work each column with its borrow: the result assembles to 35,267.

ex.main: **35,267.** A borrow chain through the middle — the check is what makes it certain.
ex.tip: Big subtractions are quiet-error country. The addition check is your floor of certainty.

questions.hint: Slide both down 1 and the zeros disappear.

ex.main: **2,238.** No borrows after the slide.
ex.tip: Check: 2,238 + 1,762 = 4,000. Round-number checks are the fastest kind.

questions.hint: The numbers are close — walk between them.

ex.main: **18.** Counting up: two hops across a tiny gap.
ex.tip: Reaching for the algorithm here would work — and take five times as long. Choosing the tool is the skill.

questions.q: Compute 8,000 − 2,996 mentally. Which way does the fix-up go?
opts: Trade 2,996 for 3,000, get 5,000 — you took 4 too many, so give them back: 5,004
Trade 2,996 for 3,000, get 5,000 — then subtract 4 more: 4,996
questions.hint: Compare what you removed with what was asked.
steps: That is 4 too many — the running answer is 4 too small.

ex.main: **5,004.** Over-removed by 4, so the answer collects 4 back.
ex.tip: The fix-up flip is THE compensation error. One spoken sentence — "I took too much, I give back" — prevents it.

questions.q: Adding 529 + 346 by partial sums, which pieces appear?
questions.hint: Hundreds alone, tens alone, ones alone.

ex.main: **800, 60, and 15 — total 875.** Every trade out in the open.
ex.tip: Partial sums is the algorithm with the lights on. Use it whenever a carry feels slippery.

opts: Left to right only: the order is fixed
Round them all and add the rounds for the exact answer
Add 31,000 + 14,250 first because big numbers go first
questions.hint: Two of these tails were made for each other.

ex.main: **55,000, by pairing the friendly two.** Order is yours to choose — choose the one with round numbers in it.
ex.tip: Scanning the endings before you add a list takes three seconds and often saves the whole algorithm.

questions.hint: Difference + subtracted amount = start.
steps: The subtraction claims 5,231 splits into 2,876 and 2,355.

ex.main: **2,355 + 2,876 = 5,231.** The check rebuilds the starting number from its two pieces.
ex.tip: One of the wrong options scrambles digits (2,867) — checks only count when every digit agrees.

questions.q: Mia claims 23,514 + 38,821 = 91,335. Judge it with an estimate.
opts: 24,000 + 39,000 = 63,000 — the claim is nearly 30,000 too high; recheck
The claim is fine because it is bigger than both addends
questions.hint: Build the estimate, then measure the gap.
steps: A 28,000 gap is not rounding noise — something structural broke.
The exact sum is 62,335, right beside the estimate.

ex.main: **Recheck — the sum is 62,335, near the 63,000 estimate.** The claim likely came from misaligned columns.
ex.tip: The estimate cannot name the error, but it can refuse to let one through. That refusal is its whole job.

questions.hint: Both numbers move down 1 together.

ex.main: **8,999 − 5,467 = 3,532.** Both ends slid, the gap held.
ex.tip: The wrong options each slide only one end — and the gap moves the moment you do.

questions.q: Subtracting 812 − 357, Kip writes 545. Diagnose and correct it.
opts: He flipped the short columns — done properly the difference is 455
He forgot the hundreds — the answer is 545 plus 100
questions.hint: Check his ones digit: where would a 5 come from?
steps: His ones digit 5 could be honest — 12 − 7 = 5 — but his tens digit 4 is 5 − 1, digits flipped instead of borrowed.
Run it clean: ones 12 − 7 = 5, tens 10 − 5 = 5, hundreds 7 − 3 = 4.
Correct difference: 455. His check would have failed: 545 + 357 = 902, not 812.
The flip error feels smooth because it never gets stuck — the check is what catches it.

ex.main: **455 — Kip flipped a column.** His answer fails the addition check by 90, and failed checks are verdicts.
ex.tip: Any subtraction answer is one cheap addition away from certainty. Spend the addition.

questions.q: Ana estimates 4,621 + 3,738 by rounding both DOWN to 4,600 + 3,700 = 8,300. What must be true of the exact sum?
opts: It is greater than 8,300 — both trades threw a little away
questions.hint: Track what each rounding discarded.
steps: The estimate is missing both scraps, so the true sum sits above it.

ex.main: **Greater than 8,300.** Two downward roundings make a guaranteed underestimate.
ex.tip: When both roundings push one way, the estimate turns into a bound — a promise about direction, not just distance.

opts: 39,215 — add the two pieces to rebuild the start
5,465 — subtract the smaller from the larger
questions.hint: The start was cut into two known pieces.
steps: ▲ was split into 16,875 removed and 22,340 left.

ex.main: **39,215.** Solving backwards is the addition check promoted to the main event.
ex.tip: Both directions matter on the test: forward to find a difference, backward to find a start.

questions.q: Which strategy fits 5,001 − 4,997 best, and what is the answer?
opts: The full algorithm — the answer is 4
Round both and subtract — the answer is 0
Slide both up 3 — the answer is 14
questions.hint: Look at how far apart the numbers are before choosing anything.
steps: The gap is 4, walked in two tiny hops.
The algorithm gets 4 too — through three borrows it never needed.

ex.main: **Count up: 4.** The right tool for close numbers is a short walk, not heavy machinery.
ex.tip: The algorithm option quotes the right answer with the wrong price tag. On a timed test, the price matters.

questions.q: Round 274,381 to the nearest ten thousand.
questions.hint: The thousands digit makes the call.
steps: Rounding place: the ten thousands — the 7.
One digit right: 4. Less than 5, the 7 stays.

ex.main: **270,000.** Topic 1 riding along, exactly as the test will make it.
ex.tip: Every estimate in Topic 2 is this skill wearing work clothes. Keep it sharp.

questions.q: How does the value of the 4 in 42,600 compare to the value of the 4 in 4,260?
questions.hint: Find each 4's place first.
steps: In 42,600 the 4 is in the ten thousands: 40,000.
In 4,260 the 4 is in the thousands: 4,000.
One place further left means ten times the value.

ex.main: **Ten times.** Same digit, one address apart, factor of ten.
ex.tip: The ten-times rule is the spine of the whole number system — it will spiral onto every test this year.

opts: < — 124 is less than 214, so flip it
= — the digits are the same set
questions.hint: March from the left to the first difference.

ex.main: **> , decided at the hundreds.** Same digits, different arrangement — the march sorts it out.
ex.tip: Anagram numbers are the march's favourite test. Only the places can tell them apart.

questions.q: Write "seven hundred thousand, ninety" as a number.
questions.hint: Two periods, lots of zeros holding seats.
steps: "Seven hundred thousand" fills the thousands period: 700,—.

ex.main: **700,090.** The words skipped many places, and zeros hold every one of them.
ex.tip: The fewer words a number name has, the more zeros its digits need. Silence means zero.

questions.q: What is the SMALLEST number that rounds to 400,000 at the nearest hundred thousand?
questions.hint: The bottom edge of the neighbourhood is the halfway point below.
steps: The benchmark below is 300,000; halfway up is 350,000.
At the school rule, 350,000 rounds UP — it is the first number in.
349,999 falls back to 300,000. So the floor is 350,000.

ex.main: **350,000.** The neighbourhood of 400,000 runs from 350,000 through 449,999.
ex.tip: Edges, always edges. These questions are never about the middle of the range.

questions.q: Theo claims: "Rounding always changes a number." Find the counterexample.
opts: 300 rounded to the nearest hundred is 300 — unchanged
256 rounds to 300, which supports the claim
450 rounds to 500, which supports the claim
questions.hint: What happens when a number is already sitting on a benchmark?
steps: It is already a multiple of 100 — the nearest benchmark is itself.
Rounded, it is still 300. The claim just died.

ex.main: **300 rounds to 300.** Numbers already on a benchmark round to themselves.
ex.tip: Always-claims lose at the boundaries: ties, self-cases, empty cases. Check those first, in math and everywhere.
